body.text: The European Commission has proposed the EU Keeping Internet Digital Spaces Accountable and Trustworthy Act, or EU KIDS Act. Presenting the proposal on September 17, commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: “Too often these addictive features are a business plan. The goal is to keep the children online and monetise their attention.”

On a school day, adolescents aged 13-18 in Europe spend an average of 4.5 hours online; on weekends, the figure rises to 6.1 hours, according to a Eurobarometer survey on teenagers’ screen use and mental health released by the commission. Fourteen per cent reported spending more than 10 hours a day on screens. Nearly one in three said social media made them feel stressed, sad, or socially excluded, while a quarter said they had encountered “harmful or distressing content” such as hate speech and pressure over appearance or body image.

The proposal would prohibit children under 13 from holding social media accounts and set 15 as the EU-wide minimum age for creating an autonomous account on specified social networking and video-sharing services. Those aged 13 and 14 could use limited, parent-supervised accounts. It would also require online services used by minors to adopt “safety by design” measures, covering social networking services, video-sharing platforms, online games, AI companions, general conversational chatbots, and software application stores. The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union will negotiate the law’s provisions, which could change before the final text is adopted.
Why is the EU acting now?

The KIDS Act is the latest step in a broader EU effort to address the risks children face online. In February 2026, the commission adopted an action plan against cyberbullying, adding to an existing child-safety framework that includes the Digital Services Act (DSA), which requires platforms accessible to minors to maintain high standards of privacy, safety, and security. The Act also follows regulatory investigations into how digital platforms are designed and how those designs affect young users.

In February, the commission preliminarily found TikTok in breach of the DSA over its “addictive design”, highlighting features such as infinite scrolling, autoplay, push notifications, and its highly personalised recommender system. The commission said these features “fuel the urge to keep scrolling and shift the brain of users into ‘autopilot mode’”, encouraging compulsive use, and had not been adequately assessed for their effects on users’ physical and mental well-being, including minors’.

The commission also preliminarily found Meta in breach on two counts. In April, it found Meta had failed to prevent children under 13 from accessing Instagram and Facebook. Although Meta’s own terms set 13 as the minimum age, its enforcement measures “do not seem to be effective”, since children could enter a false date of birth without an effective check. In July, Meta was similarly found in breach over the addictive design of both platforms.

These cases have added to growing public concern. A Eurobarometer study in July 2026 found cyberbullying and online harassment the leading worry, cited by 71 per cent of respondents, followed by online grooming and sexual exploitation at 70 per cent. Sixty-nine per cent cited harmful content, including violence, self-harm, and extremism, and the same proportion cited misuse of children’s personal data. Sixty-four per cent worried about children being recruited for illegal activities, while 60 per cent identified addictive platform design as a risk. Nearly two-thirds supported EU rules restricting children’s social media access by age.

The push for EU-wide rules also stems from differences across member states. The commission’s explanatory memorandum notes that Italy, France, Norway, Greece, Austria, Poland, and Belgium notified draft legislation restricting minors’ access to digital services in 2025 and 2026. These measures vary in scope, prompting the commission to propose a common framework that would reduce the risk of fragmented national rules across the single digital market.
What are the new age rules?

The centrepiece is an EU-wide age framework for social networking and video-sharing services that would delay “autonomous account creation” until 15 on services the commission considers capable of posing risks to minors. It is not a general ban on internet access.

Children under 13 would not be allowed social media accounts on covered services. From 13 to under 15, a parent or guardian could set up a limited account, subject to parental controls, a maximum daily screen-time limit of one hour, and parental approval of contacts. From 15, young people could create and manage their own accounts.

A narrow exception exists for video-sharing services specifically designed for children under 13: a parent could allow a child to access such a service through the parent’s own account, without an independent account for the child. Personalised feeds and search functions would be disabled, the parent would set a daily limit of up to one hour, and could stop access at any time.
The commission describes the system as a graduated approach based on children’s “evolving capacities”, with stronger restrictions for younger children and greater autonomy as they age.

Meghna Bal, director of Esya Centre, a New Delhi-based technology policy think tank, argues that restricting access during these formative years could limit how children develop identity and community. “The proposal is ensuring that parents become the gatekeepers for the online space. What happens in a circumstance where the parent is abusive? What happens then to the child? If they want to send a message out, if the online world is their only way of interacting or calling for help or something like that, what happens in circumstances like that?” she said.
What will platforms have to change?
The KIDS Act goes beyond age restrictions. For users under 18, covered services would have to meet a set of safety-by-design requirements.

The proposal would prohibit features designed to encourage compulsive or excessive use, including infinite scrolling without meaningful stopping points, autoplay, certain reward mechanisms, streaks that penalise users for not returning every day, and notifications designed to pull children back to a service. Services would also have to provide effective time limits and breaks, including measures to protect children’s sleep and school time.

Recommender systems for minors would have to prioritise safety, quality, and mental health over engagement. Personalisation based on tracking would be off by default, data from outside the service could not be used, and systems would have to include safeguards against “rabbit holes” of harmful content. Children would have an easy way to reset their feeds, including at least one option that does not rely on profiling.

Kahaan Mehta, a senior resident fellow at the Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy, said risks can arise from the ordinary operation of platforms, not only from harmful content posted by users. Compulsive use, lowered self-esteem, sleep disturbances, and effects on cognitive and social development are among them. “These are diffuse, their impact often outlasts the interaction that produced the harm, and they can often compound together. This makes design choices a crucial gate for reforming towards safety,” he said.

The proposal would also restrict how strangers can contact children. Children would not appear in contact suggestions, could not be added to groups without their agreement, and would be able to block users anonymously. Their profiles would be private by default, with geolocation, camera, and microphone access switched off by default.

Services would have to provide tools for children to block or mute other users, manage their time online, and report harmful content. Parents would get corresponding tools to set screen-time limits, manage settings, approve contacts, and report harmful content on their child’s behalf.
How will platforms check a child’s age?

Platforms would no longer be able to rely on users simply entering a date of birth. For new accounts covered by the age restrictions, they would have to use certified age-verification solutions, including a free EU age-verification app and, in time, the European Digital Identity Wallet.

The system is designed to establish whether a user is above or below an age threshold without giving the platform access to identity documents, using “zero-knowledge proof” technology that verifies age without revealing further identifying information. The proposal says age-assurance systems must not identify, locate, track, target, advertise to, or profile recipients.

Bal sees a contradiction between the proposal’s privacy safeguards and its verification requirements. “On one hand, the proposal is saying privacy, safety, and security. On the other hand, they require very invasive age-assurance and identity-verification requirements, which violate the very privacy that they are seeking to protect,” she said.

Existing accounts pose a separate problem. Platforms would have to establish whether holders are under 15 using an age-verification solution or, where they can establish with a high degree of confidence that a user is above the threshold, reasonable signals such as the date an account was created or previously acquired credit card details. Within six months of the rules becoming applicable, platforms would have to establish whether existing accounts belong to under-15s and disable accounts where users are found to be under 15 or their age cannot be established.
What about India?
As governments worldwide tighten rules on children’s use of digital platforms, India too is debating similar questions, though from a different regulatory starting point.

The Economic Survey 2025-26 flagged digital addiction among young people as a growing concern, noting that high-intensity digital use can affect study, productivity, and well-being, and called for policies to safeguard the next generation.

In March 2026, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) held a meeting on children’s access to social media, including whether access should be banned or regulated by age. The Centre was also reported to be considering a graded system of restrictions, with separate rules for children aged 8-12, 12-16, and 16-18, and a possible stand-alone law on children’s social media access. The discussion brought together government officials, academics, child-rights experts, and civil society groups.

India’s existing framework, however, takes a different approach from the EU’s. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, defines anyone below 18 as a child and requires verifiable parental consent to process a child’s personal data. It bars processing that could harm a child’s well-being and restricts tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising. Rules notified in November 2025 set out how to verify parental consent. But unlike the EU proposal, the DPDP Act sets no minimum age for social media accounts. It regulates how children’s data is processed rather than who may hold an account at what age.

A September 2026 review by the Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy mapped 34 provisions across 10 statutes and subordinate legislations against 14 forms of digital harm. It found India’s framework largely reactive and fragmented, with limited attention to children’s evolving capacities, systemic risks in digital environments, and newer or sustained forms of harm. The review states that five of the 14 harms identified fall completely outside the present regulatory architecture.

Recent cases have sharpened questions about platform responsibility. In September, the NHRC sought reports from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, and the Delhi Police after media reports alleged that paid Instagram advertisements had directed users to channels offering child sexual abuse material. NHRC asked about compliance with reporting obligations under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, and whether Meta’s AI and algorithmic systems, which generate, curate, recommend, and amplify content, raise questions about their status and obligations under existing rules.

Mehta, one of the Vidhi report’s authors, cautions against treating age alone as a sufficient measure of vulnerability. “Children are not a single category from birth to the age of eighteen,” he said. “A measure that might be necessary for a young child may be needlessly restrictive for a 16-year-old.” Vulnerability, he added, also varies with gender, sexual-minority status, self-esteem, cultural background, and socio-economic circumstances.

That variation is stark in India, where access to digital devices is itself unequal. The Annual Status of Education Report 2024 found that 82.2 per cent of rural children aged 14-16 could use a smartphone, but only 31.4 per cent had their own device. Smartphone use and ownership were lower among girls: 79.4 per cent of girls could use a smartphone, compared with 85.5 per cent of boys, while 26.9 per cent of girls owned one, compared with 36.2 per cent of boys. Among children who used social media, 62 per cent knew how to block or report a profile, and 55.2 per cent knew how to make a profile private. These figures suggest any Indian age-gating law would need to reckon with device-sharing patterns the EU proposal does not have to consider.

For some children, the internet remains an important social space rather than only a risk. UNICEF consultations with more than 200 children across seven countries, including India, found that they use digital spaces for learning, communication, self-expression, and relationships, alongside concerns about cyberbullying and hate.

Bal says age-based restrictions need to account for children who depend on online communities unavailable to them offline. “The proposal also disregards kids from marginalised groups like LGBTQIA+ who may not have any sense of community offline. They may have their entire community online, and those kids are vulnerable on both fronts. They need to have the space to interact with people of their own ilk, which they may not be able to do in an offline circumstance, particularly in a conservative household or society,” she said.

She also points to the academic pressure Indian children face, where schoolwork, tuition, and examinations leave little room for recreation. “What’s unique to India is that sometimes going online is the only escape, or the only free time or downtime, that a child has because there’s so much study pressure here,” she said. “Kids are just going online because they don’t have access to opportunities to play or just decompress offline because there is so much academic pressure.”

For Mehta, any regulatory response needs to match the evidence and the harm rather than import a template wholesale. “Regulation should be proportional to the nature, severity, and evidence of harm,” he said, arguing for binding law where harms are serious, well-evidenced, and causally linked, with softer codes, guidance, or awareness measures where evidence is still developing or diffuse. “The legal, socioeconomic, and cultural settings in which these rules operate are very different. The same measure can have very different implications in different countries.”
What about AI, online games, and app stores?

AI, an evolving part of the digital world, brings a newer set of concerns. The KIDS Act extends safeguards to AI companions and general conversational chatbots to prevent minors from being exposed to “design features and system behaviours that simulate interpersonal relations that are likely to create emotional dependencies”.

Under Article 14 of the proposal, providers of these AI systems would have to assess and test them for risks to children’s health, safety, fundamental rights, and physical, mental, and emotional well-being before deployment, and monitor harms and emerging risks after launch. Where such systems are offered through social networks, video-sharing services, or online games, they should not be activated automatically or promoted prominently to minors, and children would have to be able to opt out easily. For children under 13, access would be available only through parental-control tools.

Online games would also be subject to age-appropriate design requirements. App stores would have to assign age ratings to apps, including games, using a published methodology, prevent children from accessing or buying apps inappropriate for their age, and carry the EU age-verification tool.

Vidhi’s report identifies gaming platforms and conversational tools, including chatbots and large language models, as important points through which children engage with technology. Mehta said these are complex systems, and legislative approaches must be calibrated accordingly. “Children are right-bearers in the digital space. Therefore, where, for instance, the legislative approach may curtail children’s right to expression, association, and access to information and participation, jurisdictions must explore alternative, effective tools which can achieve the desired objective,” he said.
What happens to large technology companies?

The proposal reverses the usual burden of proof for the largest platforms. Very Large Online Platforms, defined under the DSA as services with at least 45 million monthly active users in the EU, would have to demonstrate compliance rather than waiting for regulators to establish non-compliance. Before their services come into contact with children under the new rules, they would have to submit a detailed compliance plan, which independent auditors, paid for by the platforms, would verify.

Enforcement would build on existing structures under the DSA and, for AI companions and chatbots, the AI Act. The commission would directly supervise the largest platforms and AI systems within its remit, while national authorities would remain responsible for other services, including video games that are not online platforms.

Depending on the applicable enforcement regime, fines could reach 6 per cent of a company’s total worldwide annual turnover. For services under the commission’s direct supervision, the proposal sets an expedited procedure, with preliminary findings communicated within 30 days of proceedings opening and a final decision targeted within 90 days.

Bal argues that platform responsibility needs to be matched by efforts to equip children with skills to navigate online spaces themselves. “The proposal is not preparing children for the online world. It has to be done the way we prepare children for the offline world, for example, they are taught about good touch and bad touch, stranger danger, and other things,” she said. “Although the proposal is placing the liability and responsibility on the platform, it is doing nothing to really protect the children. By equipping them with tools, such as through the introduction of a digital curriculum, these are skills that will hold them in good stead well beyond their childhood.”
What happens next?

The proposal now goes to the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union, which will negotiate its final text. If adopted, the regulation would enter into force 20 days after publication in the EU’s Official Journal and would generally start applying six months later; some provisions would take effect immediately, others after 12 months.

The commission has proposed a review of the rules by August 31, 2030, assessing how well the regulation protects children online, its effect on the EU’s internal market, and its impact on freedom of expression and information, with progress reports every four years thereafter. The proposal also provides for delegated acts and a Child Safety Committee, giving the commission a role in developing and updating some of the rules after adoption.
